subject: Indian Polity
coverage: All active Polity and Polity • PYQ IDs in the 3 November 2026 question-bank snapshot, including twelve new original practice questions.

1.title: Article 14 — Equality before law
1.overview: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to every person within India.
1.context: It is in Part III. Equality before law means no arbitrary privilege; equal protection means like cases should be treated alike.
1.who: The obligation applies to the State under Article 12; the protection is available to every person, not only citizens.
1.what: The State must not act arbitrarily. It may classify people differently only where the classification has an intelligible basis and a rational link to the law's purpose.
1.why: Equality does not mean identical treatment in every situation. Reasonable classification is permitted, but arbitrary discrimination is not.
1.significance: Article 14 is a foundation of the rule of law and is frequently used to test unfair State action.
1.exam: Article 14 applies to every person. Compare Article 15 (specified grounds of discrimination) and Article 16 (public employment).

2.title: Article 21A — Right to Education
2.overview: Article 21A makes free and compulsory education a Fundamental Right for children aged six to fourteen years.
2.context: The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 came into force on 1 April 2010.
2.who: The State must provide the legal framework and arrangements for free and compulsory elementary education.
2.what: Article 21A covers ages 6–14. Article 45 concerns early childhood care and education below six; Article 51A(k) concerns a parent or guardian's duty to provide educational opportunities.
2.why: The amendment converted elementary education from a policy aspiration into an enforceable constitutional guarantee.
2.significance: Education supports equality, participation and human development.
2.exam: Article 21A = ages 6–14 = 86th Amendment. Do not confuse Article 45 or Article 51A(k).
2.source: Constitution of India and Department of School Education & Literacy

3.title: Governor — constitutional head of a State
3.overview: The Governor is the constitutional head of a State and the formal repository of State executive power.
3.context: Articles 153–162 deal with the Governor and State executive power in India's parliamentary system.
3.who: The President appoints the Governor. The Chief Minister leads the elected Council of Ministers.
3.what: Article 154 vests executive power in the Governor, while Article 163 generally requires action on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, except where the Constitution permits discretion.
3.why: The Governor is not directly elected and is not ordinarily the day-to-day political executive.
3.significance: The arrangement combines a constitutional head with a government responsible to the elected State Legislature.
3.exam: Governor = constitutional head; Chief Minister = head of the elected government.

4.title: Election Commission of India — Article 324
4.overview: Article 324 vests control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President in the Election Commission of India.
4.context: The ECI is a permanent constitutional body established on 25 January 1950.
4.who: The ECI administers national and State-level constitutional elections. State Election Commissions handle Panchayat and municipal elections.
4.what: Its functions include superintendence, direction and control of the electoral process under the Constitution and election laws.
4.why: Independent election administration supports free and fair representative government.
4.significance: ECI = Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice-President. Local-body elections = State Election Commission.

5.title: Fundamental Duties — Article 51A
5.overview: Fundamental Duties are listed in Article 51A in Part IVA of the Constitution.
5.context: Part IVA was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. The 86th Amendment added the education-related duty of a parent or guardian, making eleven duties.
5.who: The duties are addressed to citizens and include respecting the Constitution, protecting sovereignty, promoting harmony, protecting the environment and developing scientific temper.
5.what: The duties are not generally enforceable by themselves in the same direct manner as Fundamental Rights, although laws may give effect to them.
5.why: They emphasise that constitutional democracy involves responsibilities as well as rights.
5.significance: Part III = Fundamental Rights; Part IV = Directive Principles; Part IVA / Article 51A = Fundamental Duties. There are eleven duties.

6.title: Article 155 — appointment of the Governor
6.overview: Article 155 says that a State Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under the President's hand and seal.
6.context: Article 156 says the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President and ordinarily has a five-year term, subject to that rule.
6.who: The President makes the appointment; the Chief Minister and State Legislature do not elect the Governor.
6.what: The five-year term is not an absolute guarantee because the Governor holds office during the President's pleasure.
6.why: Appointment maintains a constitutional link between the Union and each State without making the Governor directly elected.
6.significance: Remember the pair: Article 155 = appointment; Article 156 = term and pleasure.

7.title: Comptroller and Auditor General — Articles 148–151
7.overview: The CAG is an independent constitutional authority that audits public accounts and helps legislatures scrutinise government revenue and expenditure.
7.context: Articles 148–151 establish the office and outline appointment, duties, accounts and audit-report procedures. The CAG Act, 1971 supplies further detail.
7.who: The President appoints the CAG. The CAG audits Union and State accounts and performs duties prescribed by Parliament.
7.what: Article 148 establishes the office; Article 149 concerns duties and powers; Article 150 concerns the form of accounts; Article 151 concerns audit reports.
7.why: Independent audit promotes financial accountability, legislative oversight and transparency in public spending.
7.significance: 148 = office; 149 = duties/powers; 150 = form of accounts; 151 = audit reports. CAG audits; it does not approve the budget.
7.exam: Comptroller and Auditor General of India

8.title: Collective responsibility — Article 75(3)
8.overview: At the Union level, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha under Article 75(3).
8.context: India follows parliamentary government; the ministry must retain the confidence of the directly elected House.
8.who: The Prime Minister leads the Union Council of Ministers.
8.what: If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the Council of Ministers as a whole must resign.
8.why: The principle makes the executive answerable to the elected House.
8.significance: Union = Article 75(3), Lok Sabha. State = Article 164(2), Legislative Assembly.

9.title: Article 32 — Right to Constitutional Remedies
9.overview: Article 32 gives a person the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
9.context: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right in Part III and empowers the Supreme Court to issue directions, orders or writs.
9.who: The Supreme Court is the constitutional forum under Article 32. Traditional writs include habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.
9.what: It provides a direct remedy when a Fundamental Right is violated; its focus is enforcement of Part III rights.
9.why: Rights become meaningful when an effective judicial remedy is available.
9.significance: Article 32 = Supreme Court + Fundamental Rights. Article 226 gives High Courts a wider writ jurisdiction.

10.title: Finance Commission — Article 280
10.overview: Article 280 provides for a Finance Commission constituted by the President every five years or earlier when necessary.
10.context: It is a constitutional body concerned with fiscal relations between the Union and States; it normally has a Chairman and four other members.
10.who: The President constitutes the Commission. It recommends distribution of divisible tax proceeds and allocation of State shares.
10.what: It also recommends principles for grants-in-aid and measures to augment State resources for Panchayats and Municipalities based on State Finance Commission recommendations.
10.why: Recommendations help align revenue capacity with expenditure responsibilities across levels of government.
10.significance: Article 280 = Finance Commission. Article 281 = recommendations and action-taken memorandum laid before Parliament. It recommends; it does not collect taxes.

116.title: President — minimum age and qualifications
116.overview: A candidate for election as President must have completed 35 years of age.
116.context: Article 58 sets the qualifications: Indian citizenship, 35 years, eligibility for Lok Sabha membership and no disqualifying office of profit.
116.who: The candidate must satisfy constitutional qualifications; the President is elected indirectly.
116.what: The minimum age is 35, not 25 or 30. Lok Sabha membership requires 25 years and Rajya Sabha membership 30.
116.why: The rules set minimum eligibility for the highest constitutional office.
116.significance: Article 58 = President 35 years. Article 84 = Lok Sabha 25; Rajya Sabha 30.

117.title: Vice-President — ex officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha
117.overview: Under Article 64, the Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
117.context: Articles 63 and 64 create the Vice-President's office and assign the Rajya Sabha chairmanship to it.
117.who: The Vice-President presides over Rajya Sabha but is not an ordinary elected member of that House by virtue of holding the chair.
117.what: The Chairman conducts proceedings and maintains order; the Chairman ordinarily does not vote but may exercise a casting vote in a tie.
117.why: The arrangement gives the Council of States a presiding officer while keeping the Vice-President distinct from ordinary membership.
117.significance: Article 63 = Vice-President; Article 64 = ex officio Chairman. Do not confuse with the Lok Sabha Speaker.

118.title: Money Bill — Article 110 and parliamentary route
118.overview: Article 110 defines a Money Bill by reference to specified financial matters such as taxation, borrowing and appropriation.
118.context: The special procedure gives the Lok Sabha, the directly elected House, primacy over specified financial legislation.
118.who: A Money Bill can be introduced only in Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation; the Speaker certifies it.
118.what: Rajya Sabha may make recommendations within fourteen days. Lok Sabha may accept or reject them; if the Bill is not returned within fourteen days, it is deemed passed in the Lok Sabha form.
118.why: The procedure gives the elected House primacy while allowing Rajya Sabha a limited recommendatory role.
118.significance: Article 110 = definition; Article 109 = procedure. No joint sitting is provided for a Money Bill.

119.title: Constitutional amendment — Article 368
119.overview: Article 368 sets out Parliament's principal power and procedure for amending the Constitution.
119.context: Some changes are made by simple majority under provisions outside Article 368; most amendments require a special majority.
119.who: Each House must pass the Bill separately by a majority of its total membership and by at least two-thirds of members present and voting.
119.what: Specified federal provisions also require ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures. There is no joint sitting for a Constitution Amendment Bill.
119.why: The procedure balances constitutional stability with the ability to adapt; the basic-structure doctrine limits the amending power.
119.significance: Article 368 = amendment procedure. State ratification is needed only for specified federal matters, not every amendment.

120.title: 73rd Constitutional Amendment — Panchayati Raj
120.overview: The 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions by inserting Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule.
120.context: It came into force on 24 April 1993. The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects that may be devolved.
120.who: The State Legislature provides the detailed framework; the State Election Commission supervises Panchayat elections under Article 243K.
120.what: The amendment envisages village, intermediate and district levels, with constitutional provisions for reservations, duration, elections and State Finance Commissions.
120.why: It seeks democratic decentralisation by bringing local self-government closer to rural residents.
120.significance: 73rd = rural Panchayats = Part IX = Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects) = 24 April 1993. Article 243M contains special exclusions for Meghalaya.

121.title: 74th Constitutional Amendment — Municipalities
121.overview: The 74th Amendment gave constitutional status to urban local bodies by inserting Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule.
121.context: It came into force on 1 June 1993. The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 municipal subjects.
121.who: The Constitution provides for Nagar Panchayats, Municipal Councils and Municipal Corporations, with details set by State law.
121.what: Article 243ZA assigns municipal election supervision to the State Election Commission.
121.why: It provides a constitutional framework for urban self-government and civic services.
121.significance: 74th = urban municipalities = Part IXA = Twelfth Schedule (18 subjects). 73rd is rural Panchayats.
121.exam: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

122.title: Attorney General of India — Article 76
122.overview: Article 76 provides for the Attorney General of India, the highest law officer of the Union.
122.context: The Attorney General advises the Government of India and performs legal duties assigned by the President.
122.who: The President appoints a person qualified to be a Supreme Court judge; the Attorney General holds office during the President's pleasure.
122.what: The Attorney General may speak and take part in proceedings of either House and committees when permitted, but has no vote by virtue of the office.
122.why: The office provides constitutional legal advice to the Union government.
122.significance: Article 76 = Attorney General of India. Article 165 = Advocate General of a State. The Attorney General is not head of the judiciary.

123.title: Election of the President — Articles 54 and 55
123.overview: The President is elected indirectly by an electoral college under Article 54, using the method in Article 55.
123.context: The college includes elected MPs of both Houses and elected members of State Legislative Assemblies, including Delhi and Puducherry.
123.who: Nominated MPs, nominated MLAs and members of State Legislative Councils are excluded.
123.what: Article 55 prescribes proportional representation by single transferable vote and secret ballot; vote values are weighted under constitutional rules.
123.why: The method combines Union and State representation in a federal system.
123.significance: President = elected MPs + elected MLAs. It is not a direct popular vote. The Vice-President's electoral college is different.

166.title: Article 17 — Abolition of untouchability
166.overview: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.
166.context: It is part of the Right to Equality in Part III and protects dignity against caste-based exclusion.
166.who: The provision binds the State and has consequences for private conduct; Parliament has enacted laws to punish practices associated with untouchability.
166.what: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 gives effect to the prohibition; the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 addresses a wider range of offences.
166.why: It is a direct constitutional commitment to social equality and dignity.
166.significance: Article 17 = abolition of untouchability. Article 18 = abolition of titles.

167.title: Freedom of speech and expression — Article 19(1)(a)
167.overview: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees citizens the freedom of speech and expression.
167.context: The freedom supports democratic discussion, criticism, publication and exchange of ideas.
167.who: The right is guaranteed to citizens; it is not an unlimited licence to violate other rights or public interests.
167.what: Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions on specified grounds, including sovereignty and integrity, security of the State, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence.
167.why: The freedom enables accountability and informed participation while protecting other constitutionally recognised interests.
167.significance: Article 19(1)(a) = speech; Article 19(2) = permitted reasonable restrictions. It is not absolute.

170.title: Speaker's certification of a Money Bill
170.overview: Article 110(3) assigns the question whether a Bill is a Money Bill to the Speaker of Lok Sabha.
170.context: The certificate determines whether the special procedure for Money Bills applies.
170.who: The Speaker, not the President, Prime Minister or CAG, makes the certification under the constitutional text.
170.what: The Speaker examines whether the Bill contains only matters specified in Article 110(1), or matters incidental to them.
170.why: The certification determines Rajya Sabha's limited fourteen-day recommendatory role.
170.significance: Article 110(3) = Speaker's decision. A Money Bill is narrower than the general category of financial legislation.

171.title: Minimum age for Lok Sabha membership
171.overview: A person must have completed 25 years of age to be qualified for membership of the Lok Sabha.
171.context: Article 84 sets constitutional qualifications for membership of Parliament; election laws add further requirements.
171.who: The candidate must be an Indian citizen and satisfy the constitutional and statutory requirements.
171.what: The minimum age for Lok Sabha is 25; the Rajya Sabha minimum is 30.
171.why: The distinction between the Houses is a frequent static-GK question.

172.title: Minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership
172.overview: A person must have completed 30 years of age to be qualified for membership of the Rajya Sabha.
172.context: Article 84 sets qualifications for membership of Parliament.
172.who: The candidate must be an Indian citizen and satisfy constitutional and statutory requirements.
172.what: The minimum age for Rajya Sabha is 30, five years higher than the Lok Sabha minimum of 25.
172.why: The age distinction helps candidates compare the two Houses.

175.title: Vice-President — ex officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha
175.overview: Under Article 64, the Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
175.context: Articles 63 and 64 create the Vice-President's office and assign the Rajya Sabha chairmanship to it.
175.who: The Vice-President presides over Rajya Sabha but is not an ordinary elected member of that House by virtue of holding the chair.

176.title: President's ordinance power — Article 123
176.overview: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate an Ordinance when the constitutional conditions are met and immediate action is necessary.
176.context: It permits temporary law-making when Parliament is not able to legislate through its ordinary process.
176.who: The President acts on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers; the power is available when both Houses are not in session simultaneously.
176.what: An Ordinance has the force of an Act while it operates. It must be laid before both Houses and ordinarily ceases six weeks after Parliament reassembles, unless disapproved earlier or withdrawn.
176.why: The power addresses urgent situations but remains temporary and constitutionally limited.

177.title: Governor's ordinance power — Article 213
177.overview: Article 213 empowers a Governor to promulgate an Ordinance when the State Legislature is not in session and immediate action is necessary, subject to constitutional conditions.
177.context: It is the State-level counterpart of the President's ordinance power under Article 123.
177.who: The Governor acts on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers, subject to specified constitutional requirements.
177.what: An Ordinance has the force of a State Act while it operates and ordinarily ceases six weeks after the Legislature reassembles, unless disapproved earlier or withdrawn.
177.why: The power enables temporary action during legislative recess while preserving legislative control.

178.title: What is a Fundamental Right?
178.overview: Fundamental Rights are constitutional guarantees contained mainly in Part III, Articles 12–35.
178.context: They protect liberty, equality and dignity and limit State power. Some apply only to citizens; others apply to every person.
178.who: Part III includes equality, freedoms, protection against exploitation, religious freedom, cultural and educational rights and constitutional remedies.
178.what: Fundamental Rights are generally enforceable through courts. Right to Property ceased to be a Fundamental Right after the 44th Amendment and is now under Article 300A.
178.why: They protect individuals from unlawful State action and form a core part of constitutional democracy.
178.significance: Right to Equality is a Fundamental Right. Right to Property is under Article 300A, not Part III; right to vote is not generally classified as a Fundamental Right.

179.title: Supreme Court as a court of record — Article 129
179.overview: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a court of record and gives it power to punish for contempt of itself.
179.context: A court of record keeps authoritative judicial records that have evidentiary value.
179.who: The Supreme Court exercises this authority as the apex constitutional court.
179.what: Article 129 gives the Supreme Court court-of-record status; Article 215 separately gives that status to High Courts.
179.why: The status protects the authority and proper functioning of the courts.
179.significance: Article 129 = Supreme Court; Article 215 = High Courts.

180.title: High Court writ jurisdiction — Article 226
180.overview: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue directions, orders or writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose.
180.context: Writ jurisdiction is a constitutional remedy against unlawful public action.
180.who: High Courts exercise the power within their territorial and constitutional limits.
180.what: The five traditional writs are habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. Article 226 is textually wider than Article 32.
180.why: It enables High Courts to protect rights and supervise legality in public administration.
180.significance: Article 32 = Supreme Court for Fundamental Rights; Article 226 = High Courts for Fundamental Rights and other legal purposes.

3001.title: Article 254 — repugnancy on Concurrent List matters
3001.overview: Article 254 deals with inconsistency between a Parliamentary law and a State law on a Concurrent List subject.
3001.context: Both Parliament and State Legislatures may legislate on Concurrent List matters, so the Constitution provides a conflict rule.
3001.who: If valid laws conflict, the Parliamentary law generally prevails and the State law is void to the extent of repugnancy.
3001.what: A State law reserved for the President and receiving Presidential assent may prevail within that State under Article 254(2), but Parliament may later override it.
3001.why: The rule preserves national consistency while allowing a limited State-specific exception.
3001.significance: Article 254 = Concurrent List conflict; Presidential assent may create a State-specific exception but not a permanent bar on Parliament.

3002.title: Constitutional body versus statutory body
3002.overview: A constitutional body derives its existence or essential mandate directly from the Constitution; a statutory body is created by legislation.
3002.context: The source of legal authority is the key distinction, not the importance or name of the institution.
3002.who: Examples of constitutional bodies include the ECI (Article 324), CAG (Article 148) and Finance Commission (Article 280).
3002.what: A statutory body receives its powers, functions and limits from its establishing Act; an executive body may instead be created by government resolution or order.
3002.why: The distinction helps identify the legal source of a body's powers and accountability.
3002.significance: Constitutional = Constitution provides it; statutory = an Act creates it; executive = government order/resolution.

4014.title: Fundamental Rights — Part III
4014.overview: Part III of the Constitution, Articles 12–35, contains the Fundamental Rights.
4014.context: The rights are grouped around equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, religious freedom, cultural and educational rights and remedies.
4014.who: Some Part III rights apply only to citizens; others apply to all persons.
4014.what: Courts can enforce these rights through constitutional remedies, including Articles 32 and 226.
4014.why: Part III protects individual liberty and limits arbitrary State power.
4014.significance: Part III = Fundamental Rights; Part IV = Directive Principles; Part IVA = Fundamental Duties.

5007.title: Article 110 — definition of a Money Bill
5007.overview: Article 110 defines a Money Bill by listing specified financial matters.
5007.context: The definition covers taxation, government borrowing, custody and withdrawal of public funds, appropriation, charged expenditure, public-account receipts and audit, and incidental matters.
5007.who: The Speaker decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill under Article 110(3).
5007.what: A Bill is not a Money Bill merely because it has a financial effect; it must fall within the constitutional definition.
5007.why: The definition determines whether the special procedure under Article 109 applies.
5007.significance: Article 110 = Money Bill; Article 112 = Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget).

5008.title: Finance Commission — Article 280
5008.overview: Article 280 provides for a Finance Commission constituted by the President every five years or earlier when necessary.
5008.context: It is a constitutional body concerned with fiscal relations between the Union and States; it normally has a Chairman and four other members.
5008.who: The President constitutes the Commission. It recommends distribution of divisible tax proceeds and allocation of State shares.
5008.what: It also recommends principles for grants-in-aid and measures to augment State resources for Panchayats and Municipalities based on State Finance Commission recommendations.
5008.why: Recommendations help align revenue capacity with expenditure responsibilities across levels of government.
5008.significance: Article 280 = Finance Commission. Article 281 = recommendations and action-taken memorandum laid before Parliament. It recommends; it does not collect taxes.

5061.title: Article 14 — Equality before law
5061.overview: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to every person within India.
5061.context: It is in Part III. Equality before law means no arbitrary privilege; equal protection means like cases should be treated alike.
5061.who: The obligation applies to the State under Article 12; the protection is available to every person, not only citizens.
5061.what: The State must not act arbitrarily. It may classify people differently only where the classification has an intelligible basis and a rational link to the law's purpose.
5061.why: Equality does not mean identical treatment in every situation. Reasonable classification is permitted, but arbitrary discrimination is not.
5061.significance: Article 14 is a foundation of the rule of law and is frequently used to test unfair State action.
5061.exam: Article 14 applies to every person. Compare Article 15 (specified grounds of discrimination) and Article 16 (public employment).

5062.title: Article 17 — Abolition of untouchability
5062.overview: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.
5062.context: It is part of the Right to Equality in Part III and protects dignity against caste-based exclusion.
5062.who: The provision binds the State and has consequences for private conduct; Parliament has enacted laws to punish practices associated with untouchability.
5062.what: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 gives effect to the prohibition; the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 addresses a wider range of offences.
5062.why: It is a direct constitutional commitment to social equality and dignity.
5062.significance: Article 17 = abolition of untouchability. Article 18 = abolition of titles.

5063.title: Fundamental Duties — Article 51A
5063.overview: Fundamental Duties are listed in Article 51A in Part IVA of the Constitution.
5063.context: Part IVA was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. The 86th Amendment added the education-related duty of a parent or guardian, making eleven duties.
5063.who: The duties are addressed to citizens and include respecting the Constitution, protecting sovereignty, promoting harmony, protecting the environment and developing scientific temper.
5063.what: The duties are not generally enforceable by themselves in the same direct manner as Fundamental Rights, although laws may give effect to them.
5063.why: They emphasise that constitutional democracy involves responsibilities as well as rights.
5063.significance: Part III = Fundamental Rights; Part IV = Directive Principles; Part IVA / Article 51A = Fundamental Duties. There are eleven duties.

5064.title: Article 110 — definition of a Money Bill
5064.overview: Article 110 defines a Money Bill by listing specified financial matters.
5064.context: The definition covers taxation, government borrowing, custody and withdrawal of public funds, appropriation, charged expenditure, public-account receipts and audit, and incidental matters.
5064.who: The Speaker decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill under Article 110(3).
5064.what: A Bill is not a Money Bill merely because it has a financial effect; it must fall within the constitutional definition.
5064.why: The definition determines whether the special procedure under Article 109 applies.
5064.significance: Article 110 = Money Bill; Article 112 = Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget).

5065.title: Article 155 — appointment of the Governor
5065.overview: Article 155 says that a State Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under the President's hand and seal.
5065.context: Article 156 says the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President and ordinarily has a five-year term, subject to that rule.
5065.who: The President makes the appointment; the Chief Minister and State Legislature do not elect the Governor.
5065.what: The five-year term is not an absolute guarantee because the Governor holds office during the President's pleasure.
5065.why: Appointment maintains a constitutional link between the Union and each State without making the Governor directly elected.
5065.significance: Remember the pair: Article 155 = appointment; Article 156 = term and pleasure.

6104.title: Comptroller and Auditor General — Articles 148–151
6104.overview: The CAG is an independent constitutional authority that audits public accounts and helps legislatures scrutinise government revenue and expenditure.
6104.context: Articles 148–151 establish the office and outline appointment, duties, accounts and audit-report procedures. The CAG Act, 1971 supplies further detail.
6104.who: The President appoints the CAG. The CAG audits Union and State accounts and performs duties prescribed by Parliament.
6104.what: Article 148 establishes the office; Article 149 concerns duties and powers; Article 150 concerns the form of accounts; Article 151 concerns audit reports.
6104.why: Independent audit promotes financial accountability, legislative oversight and transparency in public spending.
6104.significance: 148 = office; 149 = duties/powers; 150 = form of accounts; 151 = audit reports. CAG audits; it does not approve the budget.
6104.exam: Comptroller and Auditor General of India

6105.title: 73rd Constitutional Amendment — Panchayati Raj
6105.overview: The 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions by inserting Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule.
6105.context: It came into force on 24 April 1993. The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects that may be devolved.
6105.who: The State Legislature provides the detailed framework; the State Election Commission supervises Panchayat elections under Article 243K.
6105.what: The amendment envisages village, intermediate and district levels, with constitutional provisions for reservations, duration, elections and State Finance Commissions.
6105.why: It seeks democratic decentralisation by bringing local self-government closer to rural residents.
6105.significance: 73rd = rural Panchayats = Part IX = Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects) = 24 April 1993. Article 243M contains special exclusions for Meghalaya.

6106.title: Directive Principles of State Policy — Part IV
6106.overview: Directive Principles are contained in Part IV, Articles 36–51, and guide the State in making laws and policies.
6106.context: Part IV sets social and economic goals for governance.
6106.who: Legislatures and governments use the principles as guidance when designing public policy.
6106.what: Article 37 says the principles are not enforceable by courts, but are fundamental in governance and should guide law-making.
6106.why: They guide welfare policy, equal justice, village panchayats and environmental protection.
6106.significance: Part IV = DPSP, non-justiciable but fundamental in governance. Part III rights are generally enforceable.

6140.title: Article 14 — Equality before law
6140.overview: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to every person within India.
6140.context: It is in Part III. Equality before law means no arbitrary privilege; equal protection means like cases should be treated alike.
6140.who: The obligation applies to the State under Article 12; the protection is available to every person, not only citizens.
6140.what: The State must not act arbitrarily. It may classify people differently only where the classification has an intelligible basis and a rational link to the law's purpose.
6140.why: Equality does not mean identical treatment in every situation. Reasonable classification is permitted, but arbitrary discrimination is not.
6140.significance: Article 14 is a foundation of the rule of law and is frequently used to test unfair State action.
6140.exam: Article 14 applies to every person. Compare Article 15 (specified grounds of discrimination) and Article 16 (public employment).

6141.title: Money Bill — Article 110 and parliamentary route
6141.overview: Article 110 defines a Money Bill by reference to specified financial matters such as taxation, borrowing and appropriation.
6141.context: The special procedure gives the Lok Sabha, the directly elected House, primacy over specified financial legislation.
6141.who: A Money Bill can be introduced only in Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation; the Speaker certifies it.
6141.what: Rajya Sabha may make recommendations within fourteen days. Lok Sabha may accept or reject them; if the Bill is not returned within fourteen days, it is deemed passed in the Lok Sabha form.
6141.why: The procedure gives the elected House primacy while allowing Rajya Sabha a limited recommendatory role.
6141.significance: Article 110 = definition; Article 109 = procedure. No joint sitting is provided for a Money Bill.

6161.title: Election Commission of India — Article 324
6161.overview: Article 324 vests control of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President in the Election Commission of India.
6161.context: The ECI is a permanent constitutional body established on 25 January 1950.
6161.who: The ECI administers national and State-level constitutional elections. State Election Commissions handle Panchayat and municipal elections.
6161.what: Its functions include superintendence, direction and control of the electoral process under the Constitution and election laws.
6161.why: Independent election administration supports free and fair representative government.
6161.significance: ECI = Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice-President. Local-body elections = State Election Commission.

6179.title: Fundamental Duties — Article 51A
6179.overview: Fundamental Duties are listed in Article 51A in Part IVA of the Constitution.
6179.context: Part IVA was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. The 86th Amendment added the education-related duty of a parent or guardian, making eleven duties.
6179.who: The duties are addressed to citizens and include respecting the Constitution, protecting sovereignty, promoting harmony, protecting the environment and developing scientific temper.
6179.what: The duties are not generally enforceable by themselves in the same direct manner as Fundamental Rights, although laws may give effect to them.
6179.why: They emphasise that constitutional democracy involves responsibilities as well as rights.
6179.significance: Part III = Fundamental Rights; Part IV = Directive Principles; Part IVA / Article 51A = Fundamental Duties. There are eleven duties.

6180.title: Article 40 — organisation of village panchayats
6180.overview: Article 40 directs the State to organise village panchayats and give them powers needed for self-government.
6180.context: It is a Directive Principle in Part IV; the 73rd Amendment later inserted a detailed Panchayat framework in Part IX.
6180.who: The State is directed to promote village-level self-government.
6180.what: Article 40 expresses the policy goal; Part IX supplies a later constitutional structure, subject to Article 243M.
6180.why: It links decentralised governance with constitutional policy.
6180.significance: Article 40 = village Panchayats; Article 243K = Panchayat elections; Article 243M = special exclusions including Meghalaya.

6181.title: 73rd Constitutional Amendment — Panchayati Raj
6181.overview: The 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions by inserting Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule.
6181.context: It came into force on 24 April 1993. The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects that may be devolved.
6181.who: The State Legislature provides the detailed framework; the State Election Commission supervises Panchayat elections under Article 243K.
6181.what: The amendment envisages village, intermediate and district levels, with constitutional provisions for reservations, duration, elections and State Finance Commissions.
6181.why: It seeks democratic decentralisation by bringing local self-government closer to rural residents.
6181.significance: 73rd = rural Panchayats = Part IX = Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects) = 24 April 1993. Article 243M contains special exclusions for Meghalaya.

6214.title: Article 14 — Equality before law
6214.overview: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to every person within India.
6214.context: It is in Part III. Equality before law means no arbitrary privilege; equal protection means like cases should be treated alike.
6214.who: The obligation applies to the State under Article 12; the protection is available to every person, not only citizens.
6214.what: The State must not act arbitrarily. It may classify people differently only where the classification has an intelligible basis and a rational link to the law's purpose.
6214.why: Equality does not mean identical treatment in every situation. Reasonable classification is permitted, but arbitrary discrimination is not.
6214.significance: Article 14 is a foundation of the rule of law and is frequently used to test unfair State action.
6214.exam: Article 14 applies to every person. Compare Article 15 (specified grounds of discrimination) and Article 16 (public employment).

6215.title: Directive Principles of State Policy — Part IV
6215.overview: Directive Principles are contained in Part IV, Articles 36–51, and guide the State in making laws and policies.
6215.context: Part IV sets social and economic goals for governance.
6215.who: Legislatures and governments use the principles as guidance when designing public policy.
6215.what: Article 37 says the principles are not enforceable by courts, but are fundamental in governance and should guide law-making.
6215.why: They guide welfare policy, equal justice, village panchayats and environmental protection.
6215.significance: Part IV = DPSP, non-justiciable but fundamental in governance. Part III rights are generally enforceable.

6216.title: Article 155 — appointment of the Governor
6216.overview: Article 155 says that a State Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under the President's hand and seal.
6216.context: Article 156 says the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President and ordinarily has a five-year term, subject to that rule.
6216.who: The President makes the appointment; the Chief Minister and State Legislature do not elect the Governor.
6216.what: The five-year term is not an absolute guarantee because the Governor holds office during the President's pleasure.
6216.why: Appointment maintains a constitutional link between the Union and each State without making the Governor directly elected.
6216.significance: Remember the pair: Article 155 = appointment; Article 156 = term and pleasure.

7001.title: Article 243K — Panchayat elections
7001.overview: Article 243K vests supervision and control of Panchayat elections in the State Election Commission.
7001.context: It is part of Part IX inserted by the 73rd Amendment.
7001.who: The State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor, subject to constitutional safeguards.
7001.what: The State Election Commission handles Panchayat elections; the ECI handles Parliament, State Legislature, President and Vice-President elections.
7001.why: Independent local election supervision supports regular rural self-government.
7001.significance: Article 243K = Panchayats; Article 243ZA = municipalities; Article 324 = ECI.

7002.title: Article 243ZA — municipal elections
7002.overview: Article 243ZA provides for the State Election Commission to supervise municipal elections.
7002.context: Part IXA, inserted by the 74th Amendment, deals with urban local government.
7002.who: The State Election Commission supervises municipal electoral rolls and elections, subject to the Constitution and State law.
7002.what: Article 243ZA applies the local election framework to municipalities; it is distinct from Article 324.
7002.why: It supports regular democratic elections to urban local bodies.
7002.significance: Article 243ZA = municipalities; Article 243K = Panchayats; Article 324 = ECI.

7003.title: Article 243M — special exclusion for Meghalaya
7003.overview: Article 243M provides that Part IX on Panchayats does not apply to Meghalaya, Nagaland and Mizoram, subject to the constitutional text and Parliament's power to extend provisions by law.
7003.context: The provision recognises distinct customary and tribal governance arrangements in these North-Eastern States. Meghalaya also has Sixth Schedule Autonomous District Councils in specified areas.
7003.who: The Constitution provides the special rule; Parliament may extend Part IX to the named States by law with modifications and exceptions.
7003.what: Article 243M is not an abolition of traditional institutions or Sixth Schedule councils; it is a special constitutional rule about Part IX.
7003.why: It protects distinct constitutional treatment while leaving Parliament the power to extend Panchayat provisions through legislation.
7003.significance: Meghalaya exam point: Article 243M is the key exception to Part IX.

7004.title: Article 281 — laying Finance Commission recommendations
7004.overview: Article 281 requires the President to lay Finance Commission recommendations and an explanatory memorandum on action taken before each House of Parliament.
7004.context: Article 280 establishes the Commission; Article 281 provides the reporting step.
7004.who: The President causes the recommendations and explanatory memorandum to be laid before Parliament.
7004.what: The Commission recommends; the Union considers and reports action taken. Article 281 makes the process visible to Parliament.
7004.why: It strengthens transparency and legislative scrutiny of fiscal federalism.
7004.significance: Article 280 = Commission; Article 281 = recommendations and action-taken memorandum laid before Parliament.

7005.title: Article 55 — method of Presidential election
7005.overview: Article 55 prescribes proportional representation by single transferable vote and secret ballot for the Presidential election.
7005.context: The President is elected indirectly by an electoral college, not by a direct nationwide vote.
7005.who: Elected representatives vote under weighted-value rules that reflect the federal balance.
7005.what: The single transferable vote system allows preferences to be transferred according to the constitutional counting method.
7005.why: The method balances State and Union representation.
7005.significance: President = proportional representation + single transferable vote + secret ballot.

7006.title: Election of the Vice-President — Article 66
7006.overview: The Vice-President is elected by an electoral college consisting of members of both Houses of Parliament.
7006.context: Unlike the President's electoral college, the Vice-President's college includes nominated as well as elected MPs and excludes State MLAs.
7006.who: Members of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha vote; State Legislative Assembly members do not.
7006.what: The election uses proportional representation by single transferable vote and secret ballot.
7006.why: The arrangement reflects the Vice-President's parliamentary role and ex officio chairmanship of Rajya Sabha.
7006.significance: Vice-President = both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated members; no State MLAs.

7007.title: Article 151 — CAG audit reports
7007.overview: Article 151 specifies how CAG audit reports are placed before the legislature.
7007.context: Audit reports allow elected representatives to scrutinise public money and government accounts.
7007.who: Union reports go to the President; State reports go to the Governor.
7007.what: The President or Governor causes the relevant reports to be laid before Parliament or the State Legislature respectively.
7007.why: It links independent audit with legislative accountability.
7007.significance: Union: CAG → President → Parliament. State: CAG → Governor → State Legislature.
7007.exam: Comptroller and Auditor General of India

7008.title: Article 149 — duties and powers of the CAG
7008.overview: Article 149 provides that the CAG performs duties and exercises powers in relation to Union, State and other prescribed accounts as Parliament provides by law.
7008.context: Article 148 establishes the office; Article 149 gives the constitutional basis for its functions.
7008.who: Parliament prescribes the CAG's duties and powers through law, including the CAG's Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service Act, 1971.
7008.what: The CAG audits public accounts within the constitutional and statutory framework.
7008.why: It gives the audit institution a constitutional foundation and statutory detail.
7008.significance: 148 = office; 149 = duties/powers; 150 = form of accounts; 151 = reports.
7008.exam: Comptroller and Auditor General of India

7009.title: Article 326 — adult suffrage
7009.overview: Article 326 provides that elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies are based on adult suffrage, subject to lawful disqualifications.
7009.context: The voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 years by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988.
7009.who: Eligible citizens who have attained the prescribed age may be registered as electors under election law.
7009.what: Adult suffrage provides voting rights without discrimination on grounds such as religion, race, caste or sex.
7009.why: It is the constitutional basis for broad electoral participation.
7009.significance: Article 326 = adult suffrage; voting age = 18 years after the 61st Amendment.

7010.title: President's ordinance power — Article 123
7010.overview: Article 123 empowers the President to promulgate an Ordinance when the constitutional conditions are met and immediate action is necessary.
7010.context: It permits temporary law-making when Parliament is not able to legislate through its ordinary process.
7010.who: The President acts on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers; the power is available when both Houses are not in session simultaneously.
7010.what: An Ordinance has the force of an Act while it operates. It must be laid before both Houses and ordinarily ceases six weeks after Parliament reassembles, unless disapproved earlier or withdrawn.
7010.why: The power addresses urgent situations but remains temporary and constitutionally limited.

7011.title: Governor's ordinance power — Article 213
7011.overview: Article 213 empowers a Governor to promulgate an Ordinance when the State Legislature is not in session and immediate action is necessary, subject to constitutional conditions.
7011.context: It is the State-level counterpart of the President's ordinance power under Article 123.
7011.who: The Governor acts on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers, subject to specified constitutional requirements.
7011.what: An Ordinance has the force of a State Act while it operates and ordinarily ceases six weeks after the Legislature reassembles, unless disapproved earlier or withdrawn.
7011.why: The power enables temporary action during legislative recess while preserving legislative control.

7012.title: Removal of the Vice-President — Article 67
7012.overview: Article 67(b) provides the procedure for removing the Vice-President.
7012.context: The procedure differs from the impeachment process for the President.
7012.who: Rajya Sabha initiates the resolution; Lok Sabha must agree.
7012.what: The Rajya Sabha resolution must be passed by a majority of all the then members and agreed to by Lok Sabha; at least fourteen days' notice is required.
7012.why: The Council of States has a special initiating role because the Vice-President is its ex officio Chairman.
7012.significance: Rajya Sabha majority of all then members + Lok Sabha agreement + 14 days' notice. It is not Presidential impeachment.

7105.title: Article 17 — Abolition of untouchability
7105.overview: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.
7105.context: Article 17 is part of Part III of the Constitution, which contains Fundamental Rights. It is a specific equality guarantee addressing a deeply rooted form of social exclusion.
7105.who: The constitutional prohibition binds the State and is also intended to prevent the practice of untouchability by private persons. Parliament has enacted laws to give effect to the guarantee, including the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.
7105.what: The Constitution declares untouchability abolished and makes enforcement of any disability arising from it an offence punishable in accordance with law.
7105.why: The framers sought to dismantle caste-based exclusion and secure equal civic status. Formal abolition alone is not enough; laws and enforcement are needed to address discriminatory practices.
7105.significance: Article 17 is an enforceable Fundamental Right and a key constitutional commitment to dignity and equality. It differs from Article 14's general equality guarantee and Article 15's prohibition of discrimination on specified grounds.
7105.exam: Article 17 = abolition of untouchability. Link it with the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; do not confuse it with Article 14 or Article 15.

7106.title: Part IV — Directive Principles of State Policy
7106.overview: Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in Part IV of the Constitution, Articles 36 to 51.
7106.context: The Directive Principles guide the State in making laws and policies to promote social and economic justice. They draw inspiration in part from the Irish constitutional model.
7106.who: They guide Parliament, State Legislatures, governments and public authorities when framing policy and legislation.
7106.what: Article 37 states that the principles are not enforceable by any court, but are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.
7106.why: The Constitution combines enforceable civil and political rights with policy goals intended to improve social and economic conditions over time.
7106.significance: They influence welfare legislation, public health, education, village panchayats, environment and equitable distribution of resources. Courts may use them as interpretive context while respecting the constitutional distinction between Parts III and IV.
7106.exam: Part III = Fundamental Rights; Part IV = Directive Principles (Articles 36–51); Part IVA = Fundamental Duties (Article 51A). Article 37 explains their non-justiciable status.
